items.summary: The Ninth Circuit published an opinion filed November 6, 2026, in United States v. Abdul Malik Abdul Kareem, an appeal from the District of Arizona docketed as Nos. 20-10155, 21-10315, and 24-3202. The panel reversed the district court's judgment on Count 5, a conspiracy to provide material support to ISIS under 18 U.S.C. § 2339B, holding that the government did not present sufficient evidence that Kareem intended to join such a conspiracy, and remanded with instructions to enter a judgment of acquittal on Count 5 and to resentence Kareem. The panel affirmed the district court on all other issues in a separate memorandum disposition, and Judge Collins concurred in part and dissented in part, stating he would uphold the Count 5 conviction.

items.summary: The Fifth Circuit issued an unpublished per curiam opinion affirming the Southern District of Texas's exclusion of expert witnesses whom plaintiff Erica Anderson Ross designated after the scheduling order deadline in her negligence and premises liability suit against Target Corporation, and affirming the court's subsequent grant of summary judgment to Target. The court applied the four factors used for exclusion under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1), finding that the late designations lacked substantive summaries, that Target faced substantial prejudice, and that a continuance would not fully cure it. The court also held that summary judgment was appropriate because Texas law generally requires expert testimony to establish causation of medical conditions outside common knowledge, and Ross conceded that she could not prove causation without such testimony.

items.summary: On November 6, 2026, the Sixth Circuit issued a published opinion by Judge Thapar, joined by Judge Hermandorfer, affirming the judgment of the Northern District of Ohio against Gerald M. Cook, Jr., who pled guilty to gun and drug charges and was sentenced to 248 months of imprisonment. Cook appealed the denial of his request for a Franks hearing on the warrant affidavit for the search of his home, as well as the reasonableness of his below-Guidelines sentence. The court held that Cook did not make a substantial preliminary showing of an intentional or reckless falsehood in the affidavit, that courts may consider reliable evidence outside the affidavit, including police reports, in making that determination, and that his alternative ineffective-assistance claim was premature. Judge Moore filed a separate opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment.

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed November 6, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed Fredrick Asberry's conviction on one count of conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and four counts of possession with intent to distribute, and his 222-month sentence.
